item.title: I replaced Microsoft’s default Windows apps with open-source alternatives and never looked back
item.itunes:title: I replaced Microsoft’s default Windows apps with open-source alternatives and never looked back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows comes with an app for almost everything, but that doesn’t mean I have to use Microsoft’s defaults. Over time, I started replacing the built-in tools I used every day with open-source alternatives. I found replacements that felt lighter, offered more control, respected my preferences, and in some cases, packed in features Microsoft’s apps still lack.

After living with these replacements for a while, going back to the defaults now feels like a downgrade.

I tested 8 File Explorer alternatives, but this is the one that stuck

File Pilot is the king

27
By  João Carrasqueira

Files manages my files (no pun intended) like a pro

File Explorer still has a long way to go

Files was the first app that convinced me I didn’t have to settle for Microsoft’s defaults. Compared to File Explorer, it feels much more modern, polished, and lightweight in day-to-day use. The interface is cleaner, the animations feel smoother, and the overall design fits Windows 11 far better than File Explorer does in some areas.

I especially liked the tabbed interface, dual-pane view, customizable sidebar, tags, compact overlay, and the ability to preview files without constantly jumping between different windows. There is also plenty of room to personalize the layout, appearance, and behavior without making the app feel complicated.

In comparison, File Explorer has legacy elements and inconsistent UI decisions. Files strips away much of that clutter while still giving me the tools I actually use. For browsing folders, moving files, and managing everyday storage, it feels faster and more pleasant to work with.

Files
7/10

Files is an open-source alternative to File Explorer on Windows.

See at Files $10 at Microsoft Store

Zen handles my browsing needs

It's not Chromium-based, so relax

Zen has been a much better fit for the kind of browser I actually want on Windows. Microsoft Edge is fast and capable, but over time, it has started to feel overloaded with features I rarely ask for. Copilot is built directly into the browser, and Microsoft has also added unnecessary shopping tools and other services around the core browsing experience.

Zen is based on Firefox, so you don’t need to worry about yet another Chromium-based browser looking over your online activities. It delivers a cleaner and calmer interface out of the box. If you have missed the Arc browser from the old days, you will feel right at home with Zen.

I like Workspaces for separating different projects, Compact Mode when I want maximum screen space, and Split view when I need to refer to two webpages at once.

The theming option is also top-notch, and you won’t have a hard time tweaking the browser look to your preferences. You can check my dedicated post to learn more about Zen.

Zen Browser

Zen is a Firefox-based cross-platform browser.

See at Zen Browser

ImageGlass and VLC take care of my media files

You won’t miss the Photos app

Microsoft Photos has always looked good on paper, but in everyday use, I found it slow and buggy, especially when I just wanted to open an image quickly or move through a folder full of photos. That’s where ImageGlass won me over.

It launches faster, feels much lighter, and stays focused on what I actually need from an image viewer. The company improved the entire app with version 10.0.

For video, VLC was an even easier to switch. It opens practically everything I throw at it, handles unusual codecs without making me hunt for extra extensions, and gives me far more playback controls than the default Windows experience. Subtitles, playback speed, audio tracks, aspect ratio controls, and network streams are all right there when I need them.

Together, ImageGlass and VLC cover almost all of my media needs. I now have two lightweight tools that are faster, more reliable, and much better at their respective jobs.

VLC

VLC is an open-source all-in-one video player for Windows and Mac.

See at VLC See at F-Droid See at Google Play Store

OnlyOffice has been a game-changer

Try Syncthing, too

OnlyOffice has been one of the easiest Microsoft replacements in my setup because it covers the part of Microsoft 365 I actually care about: documents, spreadsheets, and presentations. The tabbed interface feels familiar enough that I didn’t have to relearn everything, and that matters when I am switching from Word and Excel.

I can open and edit DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX files, work offline, take advantage of templates, and even use the same familiar formatting tools. For my writing and office work, it gives me most of what I need without the extra Microsoft 365 baggage.

There are still advanced Excel and PowerPoint workflows where Microsoft Office has the edge, but for everyday use, OnlyOffice has been more than capable.

As for Syncthing, I use it when I want direct file syncing between my own devices instead of depending on OneDrive. It takes a little more setup, but I like having that extra control over where my files actually live.

OnlyOffice

OnlyOffice is a featrue-rich alternative to Microsoft 365.

Download OnlyOffice
8 Windows features you should replace with third-party apps

You can do so much better

7
By  João Carrasqueira

I don’t miss the originals

I am surprised how little I miss Microsoft’s default apps now. Files feels more polished for everyday file management, Zen gives me a cleaner browsing experience, and ImageGlass with VLC covers almost everything I need for media. OnlyOffice has also proved that I don’t need to stay tied to Microsoft 365 for routine document work.

None of these apps feels like a temporary substitute or a compromise. They have become part of my regular Windows setup. Microsoft’s defaults are still perfectly usable, but these are the ones that proudly sit on my Windows taskbar.

item.title: Portainer stopped supporting its community edition, so I switched to this simpler Docker manager instead
item.itunes:title: Portainer stopped supporting its community edition, so I switched to this simpler Docker manager instead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using Docker for years. It's what enables my entire smart home stack and all the other software bits and bobs that I run. While I can manage Docker from the CLI just fine, a great graphical interface has become less of a luxury and more of an everyday convenience. It makes it easy to see what's running, restart a stack and check the logs.

Portainer has been my go-to forever, but Portainer's decision to keep Community Edition locked to the older codebase while it moves in a whole new direction has made me question whether I want to stick to it in the long run. This shift in direction is what pushed me towards Dockge. This open-source Docker Compose manager from the developer of Uptime Kuma takes a much simpler approach to container management, and it might turn out to be the best upgrade I made to my NAS.

Forget about Portainer, I use this simple tool to manage all my Docker containers on my NAS

I use Dockge to manage all my Docker containers, and I won't look back (except in some instances).

7
By  Adam Conway

Moving from Portainer to Dockge is seamless

Logs, terminal and troubleshooting without the extra steps

Credit: 

To begin with, I didn't want to migrate my entire setup in one go. My Docker setup in Portainer was built around stacks and Compose files. Dockge works much the same but with some slight differences. Each application gets its own directory, Compose file and persistent data. Dockge treats that Compose file sitting on your server as the source of truth and gives you a web interface for managing it.

That makes a big difference for the better in day-to-day use. Dockge just reads the Compose files from the disk, and exposes them directly within the interface. This is particularly useful on my NAS as I'm constantly adding, removing and testing containers. I might install something for managing media, try a new utility or spin up a service temporarily to test it. With Dockge, I can create the Compose configuration, drop it on the NAS, and have Dockge bring the stack up without needing to juggle between a text editor, SSH session and Docker commands.

Dockge's Compose editor is particularly nifty and the feature I use the most. I can open a stack, change an image tag, or just modify volumes directly within the interface. Dockge also makes it a cinch to change environment variables and deploy the updated configuration from one single screen. In some ways, it's even better than Portainer in how easy it makes it.

Unlike Portainer, which made you switch tabs to tap into the logs, Dockge's cleaner approach exposes the Compose output in real time. In fact, even the terminal is easier to access. All this means that if a container fails to start, you can see what's happening behind the scenes in real time. Similarly, fixing things is just as quick.

Look, I'm not going to say that updating containers in Portainer was complicated. But the verbiage used didn't quite make it obvious for users new to working with the software. Dockge is simpler. It just flat out exposes an update button that automatically pulls image updates via a one-click process. Underneath, it's still working with the Compose configuration that I've defined.

Dockge fits the way I run Docker

A narrower focus works better for me

I run a lot of services on my NAS. At least count I had thirty-plus containers up and running. Some of these handle media, others manage downloads. I've also got network monitors and utilities like Scanserverjs that have brought back my old scanner to life. Docker is the only way to run this in a way that's manageable and makes sense. Not just that, Docker keeps them isolated from the rest of my NAS. Compose files live at the heart of enabling this. Meanwhile, Dockge gives the visual layer to control these containers.

One of my favorite features here is that unlike Portainer, where things like Compose files are effectively written into the software using Stacks, Dockge uses standard Compose files that can be accessed via any text editor. If I ever want to move between machines, I just have to copy across the configuration and directories, adjust volume paths if needed and hit deploy.

I've recently come across one more feature that might make sense for users on multiple machines. That's Dockge Agents. Dockge agents allow you to control multiple instances of Dockge running across servers through a single interface. That's not my use case yet, but as my setup grows, I can see it being useful and, more importantly, being one more reason for me to stick with Dockge.

I'll be real here, if you were a Portainer enthusiast making use of some of the more advanced features, you might not find everything available here. That's not me though. For me, the narrower focus works just fine.

Portainer was great, but Dockge worked out to be a better fit for my Docker workflow

Even though Portainer's focus has switched over, that doesn't mean that Portainer is no longer functional. You can continue using it just the same. But I wanted to switch over to something with a bit more support. Moreover, Dockge is more aligned with how I already work with Docker.

Dockge puts Compose files at the center of the experience and is better for it. It means lesser abstraction, easy editing of configuration files, deployment and even debugging. All this means switching to Dockge has been a nearly painless and easy switchover for me that I don't regret.

Dockge

Dockge is a web-based tool to deploy and manage compose-based stacks for Docker containers.

See at Dockge

item.itunes:title: My favorite 24-year-old MMO finally got the generous free trial it deserved all along
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • FFXI's free trial is now permanent — play forever under the trial limits.
  • The level cap has been raised from 50 to 75, letting trial players progress further.
  • Trial has limits: base game only, 100k gil cap, no trading/auction, and no party creation, but you can join subscribers' parties.

I'll be honest: while everyone else is getting ready to dive into Final Fantasy XIV's upcoming expansion Evercold, I'm still stuck on the latter half of Endwalker, partly because Final Fantasy XI has been taking up all my MMO time. What can I say? It still holds up even today.

Unfortunately, its free trial was pretty archaic; you could only reach level 50 of 99, and after two weeks, you were booted off the game until you bought it. Now, Square Enix has revealed a new free trial system for FFXI, and it's much better.

Final Fantasy XI's free trial now lasts forever

The level cap has also been lifted

Credit: Steam / h.r0d

As spotted by GamesRadar, Square Enix revealed all the details on the PlayOnline website. The biggest improvement is that the free trial no longer has a time limit; as long as you're okay with the trial restrictions, you can play forever without spending a cent.

To complement this, Square Enix has also raised the level cap from 50 to 75. It may not sound like much, but FFXI pioneered the "one character can use every class" system that FFXIV thrives on; in fact, I'd argue FFXI did it better by letting players pick a primary and subjob with no restrictions. You can go Warrior/White Mage if you want. There's no viable reason to do it, but it's possible.

There are some restrictions, though. You can only use base-game content, you can't hold more than 100,000 gil, you can't use the auction house, and you can't trade. You can't create a party for others to join, but you can join a party that a paying player has made. And, worst of all, you still have to use the PlayOnline client to download and play the game. Trust me, it was made in the dial-up days, and it shows.

Otherwise, you can go ahead and try the trial for free right now. And yes, if you played the game during the old free trial and didn't upgrade, you can hop back on with your old account under the new model without paying anything.

I started playing a 23-year-old MMO that's still running, and I love it

Now with less dial-up.

item.title: I finally fixed my smart TV’s buffering, and my internet wasn’t the problem
item.itunes:title: I finally fixed my smart TV’s buffering, and my internet wasn’t the problem
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Modern home networks have reached a point where internet bandwidth is rarely the problem anymore. Most people have several hundred Mbps of total bandwidth, with 300Mbps as the median broadband speed in the US. So, if you still see your smart TV buffering your Netflix stream, blaming your ISP or plan speed doesn't help.

Instead, you should consider tweaking your TV's app settings, checking your DNS servers, and switching to a wired connection. Each change can boost your streaming performance more than buying a faster plan.

Delete your streaming app's cache

Fresh cache data can solve your streaming woes

Something most users never think about is the app cache on their TV. If you have a relatively older smart TV, low free storage can make it sluggish overall. It doesn't even have to be about storage space; often, your streaming app's cache data gets outdated or corrupted, causing your stream to stutter or freeze. Blaming your connection speed or your router hardware is natural, but misguided in most scenarios.

On Android-based smart TVs, hold the OK or Select button on the app icon, click Info or Settings, and delete the cache data on the screen that follows. On Apple TV 4K, open Settings, select the app, then delete the cache. This lets your streaming app rebuild its cache, which may improve performance.

I finally gave up on my smart TV and bought a streaming box instead

The Apple TV 4K extended my sluggish smart TV's life by a few more years.

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Change your DNS servers

It's free and easy, and gives your network a boost

Another oft-ignored router setting is the DNS server. Most people keep using their ISP's default DNS servers, unaware that they are often the slowest options available. Moreover, they can compromise your network privacy by letting your ISP send targeted ads your way. Switching to free DNS alternatives can improve overall network performance by reducing the time your router takes to convert domain names to IP addresses.

If your router's admin page doesn't let you change the DNS servers, you can do it on your smart TV instead. Open your TV's network settings, select your connected Wi-Fi network, and switch to the manual DNS option. You can safely enter "1.1.1.1" for Cloudflare DNS or "8.8.8.8" for Google DNS. Alternatively, check the fastest DNS server in your area on the DNS Speed Test website.

Switch from Wi-Fi to Ethernet

Remove Wi-Fi dependency entirely

Finally, moving to a wired connection is the biggest impact you can make on your TV's network performance. Modern Wi-Fi is fast and reliable enough, especially on Wi-Fi 6E and 7 networks, but it's still susceptible to wireless shenanigans. Occasional load spikes, peak-hour interference, and slow devices dragging faster ones down are just a few Wi-Fi problems you constantly deal with.

Switching to Ethernet can eliminate most of the network uncertainty on your TV. A wired connection always beats Wi-Fi in terms of reliability, thanks to its full-duplex nature, no radio interference, and no distance drop-off. Your streaming performance on Ethernet will always be more consistent than on Wi-Fi. If your TV's Ethernet port only supports 100 Mbps, a $10 USB Gigabit adapter can easily bypass it.

TP-Link USB to Ethernet Adapter
See at Amazon
My smart TV gets Gigabit speeds over Wi-Fi, but its Ethernet port is stuck in the past

Your TV's Ethernet port might be slower than its Wi-Fi, but it doesn't matter.

4
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Buffering on your smart TV goes deeper than you think

If your TV struggles to stream seamlessly despite a 100–300Mbps connection, speed probably isn't the problem. Wi-Fi is an inferior medium to Ethernet and will always be subject to interference, congestion, and latency. You can improve wireless performance by tweaking your settings, but if possible, moving to Ethernet is the way to go.

item.title: Claude Code's desktop GUI has one superpower the terminal version will never match
item.itunes:title: Claude Code's desktop GUI has one superpower the terminal version will never match
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Claude Code started out in the terminal, and it's still where most of the talk about it happens. Most of the guides out there assume you're sitting in front of a black window with a blinking cursor, all while the Code tab in the desktop app gets treated as the softer option for people who haven't made the jump yet. I think this is a pretty fair assessment in general since developers already live in the terminal, so a tool that meets them there makes sense.

However, plenty of folks who use Claude, or who would get real use out of it, aren't developers. It seems many open the CLI once and close it pretty fast, which is pretty much where I was earlier this year; I just assumed Claude Code wasn't my thing. Then Anthropic added Claude Code to the regular desktop app, and now half of my life runs inside it. And there's one thing I keep circling back to that the terminal version doesn't really have an answer for - it's that the Claude Code GUI has eyes.

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

Why the terminal is everyone's first reach

It's the default for a reason

There's a reason the terminal is the default, and mostly it's that Claude Code was born there. Its creator, Boris Cherny, started with a simple terminal app while he was figuring out Anthropic's API, and since it was just for him there wasn't much reason to design a UI. It stayed in the terminal because the team felt a UI wouldn't still be relevant six months later, given how fast the models were improving.

For developers, it also sits next to Git and whatever else they already run, so there's no new app to open. It can also run with nobody watching, which the desktop app can't do since it's interactive.

The trade-off for me is that Claude can't see anything it makes in there. It writes the code, then I open the file myself and alt-tab between Brave and the terminal, and I have to type out whatever looks off in my builds. You can give the terminal version eyes by pairing it with the Claude in Chrome extension so it checks things in the browser while you build, but that's more setup than I was realistically going to bother with. Plus, even if you look past the security risks of this extension, it still misses many architectural and visual features the GUI has.

I tested Claude Code against 3 open-source alternatives, and one came surprisingly close

Claude might not be the only coding agent worth using.

8
By  Anurag Singh

What Claude Code can actually see in the desktop app

The GUI's superpower is that it can look at its own work

Claude Code in the desktop app can check its own work, so I don't really have to. And what I mean here is not that I'm giving Claude 100% free rein and never checking what it does - it's that I don't have to figure out a language that I don't understand.

The desktop app has a Browser pane built into the Code tab, and Claude can open whatever it's building in there. It opens plain HTML files straight from your project folder as well (PDFs and images too), which covers pretty much every single-file wireframe I make. You just have to ensure that Browser tools are switched on to actually reap these benefits.

What matters is that Claude checks its own changes after every edit by default. It takes screenshots and inspects the DOM, which is basically the page's underlying structure, so it can tell which part of the page is actually a button. It'll also click through the page and fill in forms, then fix whatever turns up. For example, when I asked it to make a pricing page's monthly/yearly toggle actually update the prices, it flipped the switch and both labels and read the prices back after every click.

It works in the other direction too, since you can drag images and PDFs right into the prompt. For example, I dropped a screenshot of a webpage UI I liked and asked for a low-fi version of its hero, and Claude compared its result to the reference and found its own headline running about 80px wider. Later the headline collided with the art box, and Claude measured the fix right in the pane.

The pane is a proper tabbed browser too, so a reference site can sit next to your build and Claude can read and interact with it using the same tools. There's also computer use, which lets Claude open other apps on your machine and control your screen (it's still in research preview). Computer use is supported by Windows in the GUI, but not in the CLI; that's macOS-only for now.

I set up Claude Code the way its creator does, and the difference is night and day

Who better to learn from than the person who made it?

19
By  Mahnoor Faisal

What this means for people who avoid the terminal

I still can't read the code, but that matters a lot less now

People treat terminal fear like a skill issue, but from a UX point of view I think it's more of a discoverability problem than anything. A blinking cursor doesn't tell you what you can do with it. The desktop app keeps the model and permission mode right next to the send button, so a lot of guessing and confusion goes away.

I never had much hope of evaluating whether code is right, but I can tell whether a thing works, and with Claude checking its own output first, I can now actually see what it's looking at.

Also, a setup that normally lives in config files is now simply buttons. I made my wireframe skill through the settings panel without opening a single file, and connectors and plugins both get set up from menus in the app instead of a terminal. This makes small automations realistic for me, like the tool I built for renaming and sorting my screenshots. It also means that for design and UX work, I can test a clickable prototype rather than a static mockup.

Claude Code is powerful, but this one setting made it far more useful for real projects

First thing you should change in Claude Code.

By  Parth Shah

The desktop GUI gives Claude eyes

Desktop and the CLI share the same configuration and CLAUDE.md files, and running /desktop in the terminal moves a session straight into the app. But I think the Desktop GUI is seriously underrated - it's the perfect tool for non-coding tasks like computer admin, for designers who don't have a developer to work with, or for those just getting started with coding. And even if you do live in the terminal, the desktop app has eyes to check its own work, which the terminal would need extra setup for.

Claude Code started out in the terminal, and it's still where most of the talk about it happens. Most of the guides out there assume you're sitting in front of a black window with a blinking cursor, all while the Code tab in the desktop app gets treated as the softer option for people who haven't made the jump yet. I think this is a pretty fair assessment in general since developers already live in the terminal, so a tool that meets them there makes sense.

However, plenty of folks who use Claude, or who would get real use out of it, aren't developers. It seems many open the CLI once and close it pretty fast, which is pretty much where I was earlier this year; I just assumed Claude Code wasn't my thing. Then Anthropic added Claude Code to the regular desktop app, and now half of my life runs inside it. And there's one thing I keep circling back to that the terminal version doesn't really have an answer for - it's that the Claude Code GUI has eyes.

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

Why the terminal is everyone's first reach

It's the default for a reason

There's a reason the terminal is the default, and mostly it's that Claude Code was born there. Its creator, Boris Cherny, started with a simple terminal app while he was figuring out Anthropic's API, and since it was just for him there wasn't much reason to design a UI. It stayed in the terminal because the team felt a UI wouldn't still be relevant six months later, given how fast the models were improving.

For developers, it also sits next to Git and whatever else they already run, so there's no new app to open. It can also run with nobody watching, which the desktop app can't do since it's interactive.

The trade-off for me is that Claude can't see anything it makes in there. It writes the code, then I open the file myself and alt-tab between Brave and the terminal, and I have to type out whatever looks off in my builds. You can give the terminal version eyes by pairing it with the Claude in Chrome extension so it checks things in the browser while you build, but that's more setup than I was realistically going to bother with. Plus, even if you look past the security risks of this extension, it still misses many architectural and visual features the GUI has.

I tested Claude Code against 3 open-source alternatives, and one came surprisingly close

Claude might not be the only coding agent worth using.

8
By  Anurag Singh

What Claude Code can actually see in the desktop app

The GUI's superpower is that it can look at its own work

Claude Code in the desktop app can check its own work, so I don't really have to. And what I mean here is not that I'm giving Claude 100% free rein and never checking what it does - it's that I don't have to figure out a language that I don't understand.

The desktop app has a Browser pane built into the Code tab, and Claude can open whatever it's building in there. It opens plain HTML files straight from your project folder as well (PDFs and images too), which covers pretty much every single-file wireframe I make. You just have to ensure that Browser tools are switched on to actually reap these benefits.

What matters is that Claude checks its own changes after every edit by default. It takes screenshots and inspects the DOM, which is basically the page's underlying structure, so it can tell which part of the page is actually a button. It'll also click through the page and fill in forms, then fix whatever turns up. For example, when I asked it to make a pricing page's monthly/yearly toggle actually update the prices, it flipped the switch and both labels and read the prices back after every click.

It works in the other direction too, since you can drag images and PDFs right into the prompt. For example, I dropped a screenshot of a webpage UI I liked and asked for a low-fi version of its hero, and Claude compared its result to the reference and found its own headline running about 80px wider. Later the headline collided with the art box, and Claude measured the fix right in the pane.

The pane is a proper tabbed browser too, so a reference site can sit next to your build and Claude can read and interact with it using the same tools. There's also computer use, which lets Claude open other apps on your machine and control your screen (it's still in research preview). Computer use is supported by Windows in the GUI, but not in the CLI; that's macOS-only for now.

I set up Claude Code the way its creator does, and the difference is night and day

Who better to learn from than the person who made it?

19
By  Mahnoor Faisal

What this means for people who avoid the terminal

I still can't read the code, but that matters a lot less now

People treat terminal fear like a skill issue, but from a UX point of view I think it's more of a discoverability problem than anything. A blinking cursor doesn't tell you what you can do with it. The desktop app keeps the model and permission mode right next to the send button, so a lot of guessing and confusion goes away.

I never had much hope of evaluating whether code is right, but I can tell whether a thing works, and with Claude checking its own output first, I can now actually see what it's looking at.

Also, a setup that normally lives in config files is now simply buttons. I made my wireframe skill through the settings panel without opening a single file, and connectors and plugins both get set up from menus in the app instead of a terminal. This makes small automations realistic for me, like the tool I built for renaming and sorting my screenshots. It also means that for design and UX work, I can test a clickable prototype rather than a static mockup.

Claude Code is powerful, but this one setting made it far more useful for real projects

First thing you should change in Claude Code.

By  Parth Shah

The desktop GUI gives Claude eyes

Desktop and the CLI share the same configuration and CLAUDE.md files, and running /desktop in the terminal moves a session straight into the app. But I think the Desktop GUI is seriously underrated - it's the perfect tool for non-coding tasks like computer admin, for designers who don't have a developer to work with, or for those just getting started with coding. And even if you do live in the terminal, the desktop app has eyes to check its own work, which the terminal would need extra setup for.

item.title: Google reveals Gemini 4 Argon, but you're not allowed to use it
item.itunes:title: Google reveals Gemini 4 Argon, but you're not allowed to use it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We're getting to the point where AI companies can no longer hand out LLMs to the general public. A year or two ago, we saw them push out new models all the time and watched users put them to work; these days, though, the models can be so powerful that they need extensive testing and guardrails before they're given to the public.

We saw it with Claude Mythos, which is so mighty that it was only given out to select entities. We then eventually got our hands on the model with variants like Claude Fable and Opus. Now, it seems Gemini has hit the 'Mythos wall', as Gemini 4 Argon is here, and you are absolutely not allowed to touch it. Not yet, anyway.

Google Gemini 4 Argon is the most powerful version of the LLM yet

It's not quite ready for the red carpet, though

Credit: Google

As announced in News from Google, the internet giant has revealed Gemini 4 Argon. You won't find it on your personal Gemini dashboard, because, while it's very powerful and internal Google employees are already using it for day-to-day tasks, it's a little too strong for public consumption.

See, we're getting to the point where AI models pose a serious threat to the internet. We've already seen several AI models, including Gemini, breaking out of their confines and hacking into other companies' servers to achieve their goal. Handing those same models into the hands of potential criminals is asking for trouble.

As such, Google is working to ensure nobody can misuse Argon:

Defending against misuse: To prevent bad actors from using Argon for cyber or chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) attacks, the model is designed to refuse harmful requests while preserving legitimate, dual-use scientific research, as per our Frontier Safety Framework. We are strengthening the robustness of our safeguards for this launch, including improving our techniques to monitor the model’s internal activations to spot misuse.

Right now, the model is being handed to trusted defenders via the Fairwind Program, but once the company is confident that nobody can abuse Argon's capabilities, it wants to "release to developers, enterprises, and consumers, starting with paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers." It'll likely be under a different name, much like Claude Mythos becoming Fable for its public release, but Google hasn't revealed any potential name change yet, if any is even planned.

The Gemini app for Windows lets you bring up your fave AI with a simple hotkey

It comes with all the features you expect from Gemini.

item.title: My home server's CPU had a free iGPU that I disregarded for months, and it handles all my Jellyfin transcoding now
item.itunes:title: My home server's CPU had a free iGPU that I disregarded for months, and it handles all my Jellyfin transcoding now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Having spent years building, configuring, and disassembling multiple home servers, I’ve grown out of the misconception that cheap systems aren’t ideal for self-hosting tasks. That said, there are a handful of services where I prefer my expensive PCs. LLMs, especially bulky MoE models, are best run on a system armed with a powerful Nvidia graphics card and ample system RAM. Likewise, I prefer using a dedicated GPU with my Immich container, as it can drive the image manager’s machine learning tasks without tanking their performance.

Applications like Jellyfin used to be a part of this list, but everything changed when I tested the iGPU in my budget-friendly N100 SBC for my video transcoding tasks. Barring certain formats, an iGPU is actually pretty darn capable of driving hardware-accelerated transcoding workloads – to the point where it has now replaced my dedicated Pascal-era GPU.

I built a 4K Jellyfin server with Intel Quick Sync for under $200, and it's enough to replace my old GPU setup

Intel's Quick Sync is a game-changer for media transcoding tasks

4
By  Ayush Pande

I’d always assumed Jellyfin needed a dedicated GPU for transcoding

That’s precisely why I passed my GTX 1080 to my media server LXC

I’d set up my Jellyfin server ages ago and armed it with the network share housing all the movies I’d archived over the years. Since many of them are in formats that are unsupported by typical client apps, I had to look into hardware-accelerated video transcoding provisions for my media collection.

That said, Jellyfin is something that my entire family relies on for their movie nights, and I didn’t want broken drivers, random compatibility bugs, or performance issues ruining their experience. As someone who went down the PC rabbit hole around the time when Nvidia drivers used to reign supreme on the Linux compatibility front, my first choice was to repurpose my GTX 1080 as the dedicated transcoding hardware. And well, my outdated GPU served my PVE-powered Jellyfin LXC without any issues.

However, I’ve recently started tinkering with self-hosted LLMs, and despite its ancient, non-Tensor design, this beast could drive Gemma-4-E4B (and even Gemma-4-26B-A3B via MoE offloading) at respectable token rates. So, I wanted to free this card from its Jellyfin shackles and relegate it to my LLM workloads. Plus, leaving a full-on gaming GPU running during Jellyfin movie nights would drain quite a bit of energy, and considering all the devices in my arsenal, I'd love to save as much as I can on my energy bills.

As such, I needed an alternative to power my video acceleration tasks, and that’s when I decided to turn my attention to a lightweight N100 server and its iGPU.

Turns out, a “mere” N100 can handle transcoding tasks fairly well

And it’s all thanks to the Quick Sync Video core built into this budget processor

With the Intel N100 being a budget-friendly embedded processor, its iGPU can’t hold a candle to a dedicated graphics card for gaming, machine learning, and LLM-hosting tasks. But if we leave these intensive tasks aside, the situation is quite different when it comes to video transcoding. You see, Intel crams the Quick Sync Video core into the iGPUs of most modern processors, which is designed to handle transcoding tasks.

I’d been using my N100 compute module (specifically, the Latte Panda Mu) as a spare PVE node for my monitoring services, and I figured I could put its QSV capabilities to the test by simulating some Jellyfin streams. Thanks to the Jellyfin LXC deployment command on the Proxmox VE Community Scripts repo, GPU (or rather, iGPU) passthrough worked automatically on this container.

Performance-wise, my Jellyfin LXC + iGPU combo can transcode eight 1080p streams as long as I don’t keep it engaged in random PVE experiments. Heck, it can even handle three 4K streams at the same time, which is way more than my family would ever need. Since it’s an iGPU on a tiny embedded processor, I don’t have to worry about the system consuming dozens of watts just to stream an old movie to my projector.

Of course, this setup has a minor caveat. While it can handle H.264 (AVC) and H.265 (HEVC) transcoding with ease, things are different when I toss movies in the AV1 standard. Since it includes an AV1 decoder, it can turn any movies that rely on this compression standard into AVC/HEVC without any issues. But since it lacks a dedicated AV1 encoder, I’d have to rely on software encoding when streaming these videos.

Personally, most of my titles are in the H.264 and HEVC formats, and I don’t necessarily have to decode anything into AV1 at the moment. So, it’s not that problematic for my setup, and I’m more than happy letting my N100 tackle my hardware-accelerated transcoding workloads while my Pascal-era GPU powers useful LLMs for my productivity services.

Intel CPUs also have another neat trick up their sleeve for home servers

Besides offering terrific performance in transcoding operations, modern Intel processors are just as capable at driving AI features in NVR platforms thanks to OpenVINO. Essentially, it’s a toolkit that makes Intel graphics cards, iGPUs, and NPUs proficient at object detection tasks. I currently use the official Raspberry Pi AI Kit with my Frigate setup, but OpenVINO detectors mesh incredibly well with cheap Intel processors, to the point where even Frigate recommends picking them up over Coral Edge TPU modules.

Intel Quick Sync is the reason I will never buy another Nvidia card for my Jellyfin server

item.title: You can now play the original Halo for free in your browser with 128-player multiplayer
item.itunes:title: You can now play the original Halo for free in your browser with 128-player multiplayer
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • An unofficial browser port of Halo: Combat Evolved supports 128-player multiplayer and split-screen co-op.
  • The game runs poorly on iOS and Android, and PC is recommended for best performance.
  • The port had 20K plays in 5 hours across 115 countries.

To say that the Halo series has struggled over the past few years would be a significant understatement. In fact, the iconic franchise has faced so many issues that Microsoft recently basically shut down Halo Studios (formerly 343 Industries) and handed over the series' development to Activision.

On the plus side, you can now play Halo: Combat Evolved for free in your web browser with 128-player split-screen co-op and multiplayer, courtesy of X user @michellhynes (Michaell Hynes) (via Gamingbible). Yes, you read that correctly. That said, Hynes still considers the multiplayer feature "untested."

Hynes also says his very unofficial browser port of Halo: Combat Evolved doesn't run well on iOS or Android, and that playing it on a PC is the best route. Still, it's impressive the 26-year-old game runs in a browser at all, and given I consider Halo: Combat Evolved one of my favorite video games ever, it's a bit of a trip to see it running in a browser.

Unsurprisingly, this unofficial OG Halo port is pretty popular

It's likely it won't be online for very long

Hynes says that in the browser port's first five hours online, nearly 20,000 instances of the game were played across 115 countries, with an average of 94fps. It works pretty smoothly, though. In the few minutes I played the browser port of Halo Combat: Evolved, the experience was surprisingly solid, though I did run into a very brief bit of lag.

item.title: Emulation already solved the problem DLSS 5 is selling, and it did it for free years ago
item.itunes:title: Emulation already solved the problem DLSS 5 is selling, and it did it for free years ago
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It seems like every other day, I find new games to inject DLSS 5 into. Whether it's by forcing DLSS 5 through ReShade or replacing a game's DLSS files with the Neural Rendering variants, it's been an absolute joy to see my childhood games transform in real time. After all, that's what DLSS 5 has been doing — "transforming" old games and basically handing out free remasters.

That's exactly what my chain of thought was as I pushed DLSS 5 into my old PS2 and PS3 games, only to realize that the free "Remasters" Nvidia's new expensive tech has been handing out are something emulators have been providing for years now, and that too, for free.

Make no mistake — DLSS 5 is remarkably good at making the past look new again, but the PC gaming community has been doing that for years without needing an RTX GPU at all.

I ran DLSS 5 on my PS2 games, and they finally looked like I remembered them

Nostalgia, meet neural rendering

11
By  Samarveer Singh

DLSS 5 is selling more than just "sharper pixels"

The real trick is making old-looking games feel new again

It's easy to think of DLSS 5 as another glorified upscaler, but that undersells what Neural Rendering is. Instead of taking a lower-resolution image and making it cleaner, DLSS 5 uses AI-generated detail and lighting information to make the final image feel considerably more sophisticated than the underlying render would suggest.

Throw DLSS 5 at an older game and you'll immediately understand the difference. Running a 2006 game at 4K will make its jagged edges disappear and lend it a surface layer of cleanliness, but it won't even touch the ancient assets. DLSS 5, on the other hand, effectively reinterprets parts of the image on its way to the screen. That's why my own experiments with Nvidia's Neural Rendering felt like I'd applied a modern visual treatment to my older games.

Now, DLSS 5 giving older games a second wind is a completely different direction from using it in future games that will be designed with native support. In that way, the same technology answers a completely different question, only this time, I've already seen it answered somewhere else, and rather effectively at that.

I put DLSS 5 on my entire desktop, and it showed me neural rendering's real limits

DLSS 5 Live Flow promised to transform my desktop — here's what actually happened

3
By  Samarveer Singh

Emulation was already breaking those limits

RPCS3 has been turning old games into remasters without neural rendering

I recently applied DLSS 5 to my old PS3 titles on RPCS3, and yes, it required plenty of hoops to jump through. From finding the right DLL and using ReShade to emulate motion vectors for DLSS 5 to latch on to, DLSS 5 on RPCS3 was rewarding but complicated. There was, however, one thing that stood out rather remarkably for me.

After I set up the emulator properly, I realized that RPCS3 itself gave me plenty of GPU-specific emulation options. The original PS3 may never have been able to output anything over 1080p, but RPCS3 immediately runs games at 1440p, 4K, all the way up to 5760p. The emulator also supports in-built upscaling, with support for AMD's FSR. With other features like Anti-Aliasing, 16x Anisotropic Filtering, and having control over which shader to use, it was immediately clear that the emulator was already giving the game a remaster itself.

Please ensure you only ever use your own games and dump your own files for emulation on PC.

And that's even before we talk about the plethora of patches available in RPCS3 for every single game. Community patches that are already available in the emulator can push compatible games beyond their original 30 FPS targets. Then, widescreen patches remove another limitation. Click on any game, and you'll be able to see mods and patches for better texture filtering and renderer improvements that can clean up the image significantly.

Then there are texture packs, shader modifications, lighting tweaks, and other community projects. None of this needs an RTX GPU or a proprietary neural model. The PC simply has more hardware available than the console did. The emulation community has spent years taking games locked to 2006-era hardware and going beyond those limitations. DLSS 5 doesn't do the same thing technically, but the philosophy behind the transformation is more or less the same.

I pushed FSR 4.1 and DLSS 4.5 to their limits on older hardware, and one changed my mind about 4K gaming

It was neck-and-neck, until it wasn't

6
By  Samarveer Singh

Emulators don't really need DLSS 5

DLSS 5 will always be "nice to have" instead of a "need to have"

Even with the emulator up and running, I have a whole host of graphical upgrades at my disposal. Games like Gran Turismo 5, Tekken Tag Tournament 2, and Demon's Souls look way better than they had any business looking at on a 2006-built PlayStation 3. I can upscale all the way up to 4K and get cleaner shadows and textures — there's your free remaster, all without losing 50% of your frame rate.

I'm not calling DLSS 5 completely pointless. It's certainly remarkable, and I myself can't stop having my fun with it. In fact, DLSS 5 does make a pretty strong case for itself because it gets a lot of the work out of the way. If I'm using DLSS 5 on an old emulated game, I can just have the Neural Rendering layer sit inside the rendering pipeline and handle part of that transformation automatically. That way, I don't really have to hunt down patches, install texture packs, configure the emulator, and then spend an entire evening if something breaks.

Of course, if you do put in the work, the emulation community has indeed solved the problem through control (while Nvidia took an inference-based approach). The former approach gives me, the user, the tools to rebuild the presentation myself, while the latter makes the machine understand what that presentation should look like.

RPCS3
See at Official Website
DLSS 5 is further proof that rasterization’s days are numbered

For better or worse, rasterization continues to be buried, and it won't be long until games are unrecognizable

74
By  Ty Sherback

The future of graphics has a funny habit of looking familiar

The emulator community never needed Nvidia to tell it that games could be pushed further than their original versions.

DLSS 5 highlights something that PC gamers have understood for a very long time now — a game's original hardware limitations don't necessarily have to define its final form. Once you give enthusiasts enough control, they will spend years finding ways around those limitations.

The emulator community never needed Nvidia to tell it that games could be pushed further than their original creators intended because they were already doing it. Nvidia may have found a way to make the process considerably more automatic and (annoyingly) more impressive.

item.title: I compared my Claude Code workflow to a beginner's, and some of my habits were making things worse
item.itunes:title: I compared my Claude Code workflow to a beginner's, and some of my habits were making things worse
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Initially, you'd scroll through social media (or Google) and come across the occasional AI tip or clever prompt someone swore changed their workflow. Occasional is, well, no longer the word I'd use. Now, every other person is a self-proclaimed AI expert. You'll find endless advice on how the right prompt should be structured, what features should be enabled and disabled, which tools you absolutely need to install, and which workflows will supposedly turn an AI coding agent from decent into indispensable.

Now, I'm someone who puts on two hats when I'm testing these tools. I'm either using them as a regular user trying to get work done with them or as a journalist who writes an insane amount of articles daily on AI trying to look for something worth writing about. The first version of me is naturally curious about every new trick, plugin, workflow, and “you’re using it wrong” post I come across. The second just wants Claude Code to do the job well without turning the setup itself into a project.

I've now reached a point where those two versions of me are starting to clash. My Claude Code setup has accumulated enough extras over time that I can no longer tell which ones are actually helping and which ones are just there because someone, somewhere, convinced me they were essential. So I decided to strip things back and compare my usual setup against something much closer to what a beginner would use.

I was keeping far too many MCP servers around

More tools, more problems

I've talked a bunch about how one of the best ways to bring AI into your actual day-to-day workflow is by connecting it to the tools you use every day. Most AI tools, including Claude Code, give you two ways to do that. You can either rely on built-in integrations where they're available, or connect external services through something called Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Well, I sort of went overboard with MCP servers. You can't blame me, though! Once you realize how many services can be wired into Claude Code, it's very easy to start treating every new connection like an upgrade. At one point, I had MCP servers hooked up for practically everything I could think of.

There were community-built ones for NotebookLM, connections for tools like Adobe, Canva, Notion, Slack, and Gmail, and then all the more obvious developer-focused ones for GitHub, databases, Vercel, and Playwright. I even had some tied into tools I use for meetings, like Read AI.

The problem is that more connections don't automatically make Claude Code better. Every server adds more tools Claude potentially has to choose between, and when several of them overlap, that can make tool selection messier rather than more useful. Before Claude Code's Tool Search started deferring tool definitions until they were actually needed, this could also eat a huge chunk of context before you'd even typed a prompt!

I kept adding memory layers Claude Code didn’t need

Turns out, forgetting can be useful

Speaking of MCP servers and adding more, memory was another area where I fell into the same trap. I figured the more Claude Code remembered about my projects and previous sessions, the better it would get.

So I ended up with tools like claude-mem and claude-memory sitting on top of Claude Code’s own built-in memory features. Not only were these memory-related plugins contributing extra instructions, Skills, and agents before I’d even typed a word, the bigger issue was the usefulness of that memory itself.

A memory system can preserve something that was true three sessions ago but no longer reflects the current state of a project. At that point, Claude has to spend time reconciling what it remembers with what’s actually in the repo, and there’s always the risk that stale context nudges it in the wrong direction.

Besides, a lot of the tasks I'd use Claude for would be in the same directory, but there really weren't that many useful connections between them. Just because two sessions touched the same project didn't mean context from one was going to help with the next. In a lot of cases, it was simply more information for Claude to sift through!

I was stuffing far too much into CLAUDE.md

My instructions needed instructions

I've written a lot about CLAUDE.md files. They're one of the easiest ways to shape how Claude behaves across a project and, as someone who has gotten tired of Claude Code forgetting my instructions, I naturally kept adding more to mine.

Coding conventions, workflow preferences, reminders, edge cases, things Claude got wrong once that I never wanted it to get wrong again, and so on. You'd genuinely find everything in there. Unlike MCP servers, the CLAUDE.md file is something that's carried into the project context every time, which means bloating it has a much more direct cost.

Claude Code works best when you stop asking it to code

Claude Code became far more useful once I stopped treating it like a code generator and started using it to understand projects and terminal chaos.

11
By  Jeff Butts

I started noticing that the longer the file got, the less reliable some of those instructions became. Important rules would get buried among dozens of things that had nothing to do with the task at hand, old guidance would stick around long after it stopped being relevant, and instructions written for one kind of work would bleed into completely unrelated tasks.

That lines up with Anthropic's own guidance too. It recommends keeping CLAUDE.md files relatively short, since longer ones consume more context and can actually hurt instruction adherence! So, I've gone back to the basics of using mine for the things Claude needs to know every time rather than as a permanent archive for every preference I have.

Not every Claude Code task needs Plan mode

I was planning two-minute tasks like product launches

Claude Code's Plan mode is something I've always appreciated.
